speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, October 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Greene that Bill C-4, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

Mr. Speaker, in 1948 the original Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was passed. It was designed to be a very temporary measure to aid mining communities throughout Canada while they passed from a period of wartime, with its shortage of men and materials, into the new era that was developing in our country, an era when the mining industry, particularly the gold mining industry, found itself in difficulty. I think everyone who participated in the passage of the original act thought that the measure would bring forth other measures of a more permanent nature to solve the problems of the gold mining industry.
The reason the country was so concerned about the gold mining industry was that during the war the industry had lost many of its employees and had had difficulty buying equipment and simple requirements such as hoses, drills, steel, machines and so on. The hope was that the mining industries of Canada would return to their former condition, prior to the war. I am sure many members here are unfamiliar with the role played by the gold mining industry in the years prior to the war. I remember when most of the employment in northern Ontario was in the gold mines. People came from all over Canada to work in the industry. Wages were considerably higher than those of other industries in the country. A salesman in a gold mining community could expect to make money on his sales, something that was almost impossible in other parts of the country.

October 29, 1970
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act We believe that we built Toronto. There are those who disagree, but nevertheless we believe that we supplied most of the money that built Toronto, and in turn that there is an obligation by Toronto that has not been met. The fact is that the gold mining industry was a key industry in the late depression years. Without the industry>
the depression would have been much more severe in Ontario. Therefore, in 1948 when mines were being closed as a result of economic conditions during the post-war years it was only reasonable that this measure was passed to assist the industry.
I am sure that no one who participated in passing the act in 1948 expected it to stay in existence for longer than three years, which was the original period, but several things happened to make it impossible for the gold mining communities to return to the economic level they had attained prior to the depression. For one thing, the product of the gold mining industry is a national commodity. All newly-mined gold in Canada is sold to the Canadian Mint, and the Canadian government in turn sells that gold, or most of it, to the United States which deposits it in Fort Knox where it becomes part of the international money system of the world.
While the cost of every other commodity has gone up, with the resultant effect this has had on the gold mining industry as on every other industry and individual in Canada, the price of gold itself has not changed. I do not intend to make a speech about the gold standard because a number of Socialist colleagues sitting behind me are not known for their great love of monetary metals. However, I think it is important to ask what role gold plays in our monetary system.
Since 1948 the government of Canada has paid out a subsidy of $281 million to the industry, and this is a period of 22 years. I think everybody who is interested in the payment of subsidies should ask why the Canadian government has been willing to sell gold at $35 an ounce to the U.S. treasury when it costs them a subsidy of $281 million to ensure the continuance of gold mining. We have now reached the stage where today 28 mines employ a total of roughly 7,300 gold miners. We shall be paying $14 million this year by way of subsidy to the industry. If that sum were divided among those employees, it would go a considerable distance toward providing them with an income to stay at home.
No one has decided what relationship gold has to the International Monetary Fund or what value there is in continuing to mine gold. I am sure there are some who do not realize the contribution made by the industry in post-war years which enabled the Canadian treasury to sell gold to the United States in return for U.S. dollars, at a time when this currency was badly needed to develop areas of Canada.
The industry presented a brief to four ministers and members of Parliament last June. They pointed out in their brief that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act had been responsible for keeping in existence most of the gold mining communities. Not only did it help maintain jobs, but part of the general subsidy sustained 
long-established communities that were facing serious
threats to their continued existence.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I am sure some people ask why we bother to keep these communities in existence. It is very interesting to note that in most of the major mining communities in Canada where gold mining has been subsidized over the last few years, changes have taken place. This would indicate that there will be an end to the type of assistance the federal government has supplied under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I am thinking particularly of the town of Timmins. Originally Timmins was one of the largest gold mining camps in North America. It produced a great deal of gold for the monetary system of North America and it was developed almost entirely around the gold mining industry.
I can remember when one of the mines in Timmins had close to 5,000 employees. Each employee was making 52 cents an hour on the surface, and when I first started, 58 cents an hour working underground. That does not sound like very much money today, but in those days they were among the highest paid employees in the country. Over the years, as other industries have developed in the mining field, gold mining wages have remained notoriously low. Very little of the subsidies has gone directly or proportionately into the wage structure. In Timmins we now have one of the largest copper producers in the country. We also have several large asbestos producers. We also have producers of zinc, lead and base metals. Even the McIntyre Mine, which is known all across the nation and across the world, has been able to develop a copper property inside the old gold-producing area, so that the same facilities are now being used to produce copper and gold.
Changes have taken place and some advantages are enjoyed in the communities because of new methods. This has only been possible as a result of maintaining the gold mine over a period of time in order to keep up the communities vital to any mining taking place in the area. The situation at Kirkland Lake is very similar. In 1957, when I was elected, there were probably nine gold mines in Kirkland Lake but today there are only two. We have added to that mining area a copper producer, an iron producer and in the immediate periphery we have developed several other base metal mines. Although the area is not self-sufficient, it is heading in that direction as the gold mining industry fails.
I have been told by the industry, as certainly the committee that met with them was told, that it is their opinion that in the very near future-in mining, that means in the next five years-world gold production will probably be used solely for industrial purposes with very little gold being made available for monetary purposes. I am not making a financial speech on financial matters, because I certainly am not capable of doing so. Since I have been a member of this House I have found that very few people are capable of making such a speech, and most of them are not here now.
October 29, 1970

It seems to me there is a relationship between gold and world trading. We have always been very happy to sell wheat to Russia because Russia did not pay us, as some other countries did, with money which we loaned them on a long-term basis to be paid back to us in bits and pieces. Russia paid us in gold bullion. We were very fortunate in this regard because we could accept that gold at $35 an ounce, hold it for a short period of time and then sell it to the United States at a profit of $7 per ounce. Perhaps we should deduct that profit from the subsidies we have paid. This might reduce them to some extent. This side of the gold mining industry is one we have not explored. I am not sure that the Bank of Canada has ever known what to do with gold. I do not know who the bright guy was in the treasury board who a few years ago said we should start hoarding gold and establish our own stockpile. But this paid off; it was a good move. There must be some smart financial people who are not in that field now because the price of gold on the international market is very little higher than $35 an ounce.
As far as the gold mining communities are concerned, they are still selling gold at a fixed price. The price has been fixed for many years. This industry, unlike any other, is not able to take advantage of the marketplace to meet higher costs, higher wages and higher maintenance expenditures. In northern Ontario, particularly in my part of the country, we have tried a number of schemes over the years. I was very pleased to hear the minister say when he introduced this legislation that there were strings attached. He said this is the time for municipalities, labour unions, employers and the gold mining industry itself, as well as the provincial government, to cooperate with the federal government in finding some way of solving the problem that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was established to solve. I congratulate him for coming to this conclusion. I came to this conclusion before I came to this House when I was working in the gold mines.
When I first started working in the gold mines, the industry made a good profit on each employee. This good profit has not been made on each employee for a long time. The industry has just got by, but has been doing a service to communities and to itself. If you think in terms of a woman who likes to be kept in the manner to which she has been accustomed, the gold mining industry has been accustomed to a fairly high standard but it is not now being kept in that way. The gold mining communities are willing to participate with the federal government in its attempts to find a solution.
We not only have the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; we have the incentives program and assistance to northern minerals exploration. The industry is asking that this program be extended to the whole of Canada and that more money be put into the fund so that finances can be provided for exploration in all parts of Canada rather than in the Yukon and Northwest Territories only. Assistance in the form of incentives has been of help, but it has not been directed in the proper way. If
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act it is to be directed to the mid-Canada corridor, where most of the development is taking place, we will obviously require much stronger incentives than we now have. It is all right to hold out a carrot to entice industry, but what industry do we expect to entice? We do not find anyone coming to nibble at the carrot.
We can offer to supply new development companies with services such as water, sewage, fire departments, schools and all the modern facilities of a big city at about one one-hundredth of the cost of these services in our major cities. But it seems to me that if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) is going to hold out to these communities a carrot in a form other than subsidies, he will require the co-operation of four or five branches of government which would have to decide that certain industries would be better off in these areas than in our major cities.
* (9:30 p.m.)
This was done in England in two ways. First, the industry was told that the undistributed profits of the company could not be used unless the company had a lease, and that it could obtain a lease only if it were prepared to move into the area to which the authorities wanted it to move and, secondly, it would not be granted a building permit in any area other than the one designated. I know this plan did not work 100 per cent. But industries were enticed to go beyond the periphery of London, Coventry and other major points and settle in areas such as the Midlands which had gone out of textile production. Heavy industries were brought into these areas, with some success.
I should like the minister to table the interdepartmental report he received. This was prepared not only by his department but, I understand, by a number of departments. The gold mining industry is not like any other industry; its problems are different. I am not particularly concerned about the 20, 25 or even the 40-year old people in the gold mining industry. We are concerned about the 50 per cent in the industry who are over 50 years of age. They have only a limited educational background and over the years they have been trained only in lode mining.
Although there are other mines in the area, the miners cannot work in them because of the dissimilarity in mining methods. Originally, gold and silver mining was carried out by one or two miners in an isolated area almost entirely on their own initiative, although supervised by others. This situation is not duplicated in other areas of mining. So the gold mining industry is in serious difficulty and, more importantly, the communities that have been built up around the industry are in serious difficulty.
In my opinion, the mid-Canada corridor concept mentioned by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) the other day in this debate is a matter to which the government should give serious consideration. Here we have a plan developed by private initiative, which indicates the immense potential of the mid-Canada

October 29, 1970
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act corridor. It indicates to the general public that those who invest money in the mid-Canada corridor will reap immense financial benefit. I have absolutely no interest in Mr. Rhomer running a large portion of Canada. I am not the least interested in giving him that large section of Canada, but I think the government should not neglect the study he has made and the information he has given concerning the immense potential of this area. I suggest, as the minister mentioned, that the gold mining communities are centrally and strategically situated in this area. They would be the basis for any organized development in that part of Canada.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) indicated that growth centres would be established. If he has pursued that policy very far, the results have missed me because in northeastern Ontario the growth centres obviously will be the established mining communities which have immense quantities of social capital. They have houses and all the amenities of the major cities. In most of these communities there are educational facilities the equal of any in Canada. In my opinion, for the employment factor we have in these communities today the facilities are far in excess of their needs.
I do not think a man who has worked for 30 or 40 years in the gold mining industry can be retrained mentally or even physically. He cannot be retrained to work in an office or even to do factory-type work. Over the years he has worked in that area and has educated his children, who cannot find employment in the area. He has worked in order to build a home for himself and his family. He has roots in the community and has made a contribution to the social capital of the community. Now he is faced with the almost immediate closing of all the gold mines if the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act are not continued.
I believe those who say that the subsidy is rather silly will have to come up with an immediate solution to take care of the people who will be displaced almost immediately if emergency gold mining assistance is cut off or curtailed. So I am looking forward to the meetings of the committee to which this bill is to be referred and to hearing the views of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in respect of the bill and his discussions with people in the mining communities concerning a solution to this problem.
The people in the mining communities today are not particularly happy with their record in respect of welfare. Kirkland Lake is the highest welfare area in the province of Ontario, with Timmins a very close second. They are not proud of these statistics or of the fact that the mining communities are dependent upon the federal government for emergency gold mining assistance to enable them to continue in existence-not to make their industry viable, but just to keep them there at all. What we want is an opportunity to expand Kirkland Lake. Every year in the past 30 years Kirkland Lake has lost a small portion of its population. We have reached the goal of the many young people today who say that we should 
have a population increase of zero. We have done a little better. Because of the facilities we have, the fact that we own our own railway in northern Ontario, the fact that we have good highways and have commodities other than the products of mines, we should with the assistance of the government be able to develop a viable community.
If the government could come up with a well thought-out, well planned and well founded policy that would have hope of success, the people of northern Ontario would owe the government a vote of thanks. The people of the gold mining communities are not happy that they have to come before the public every two or three years and request the continuation of the subsidy for a commodity which most Canadians believe should be left in the ground.
On behalf of the people of these areas, I say that I do not believe they have anything to be ashamed of, because the contribution of the gold mining communit.es to the economy of Canada and the development of the provinces in which the gold mines are situated is a very great one. Because of this I believe these people deserve support in respect of the passage of emergency gold mining assistance legislation.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
If I am at all unhappy about this bill, it is because we have retained the word "emergency" in its title. It seems to me, and it has seemed to me for some time, that anything that goes on for 22 years is no longer an emergency but is a fact of life. I am an optimist, although not sufficiently optimistic to buy gold mining stock; but I am always hoping that the international price of gold will go up.
I am sure that if the world continues in the unsatisfied and unsettled condition which exists in almost every part of the world, there will continue to be people putting gold under their beds and it is possible that the price of gold will go up. I suggest that if it goes up sufficiently high to enable mining communities to exist on their profits, they will be able to pay back to the rest of Canada many times over the contribution people have made to them over the years, because as the situation in the world deteriorates it is my opinion that gold will again become a very valuable international trading commodity.
I hope members of the House will find it easier to support the contribution that will be made under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act than wait for the day when an increase in the price of gold will make it possible to expand this industry.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks concerning this bill will be brief, because although at one time my constituency was a major producer of gold, that is no longer the case. There are many abandoned gold mines throughout the area, but the last of these closed down in the spring of this year and salvage operations are now under way. So I am pleased

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act should be allowed to retire in the communities in which they have spent so much of their lives, and some of the profits of the companies should be made available to allow them to retire in an acceptable manner.
Provision should be made for some sort of severance pay and also for some sort of payment to communities which have lost this industry. The aim should be not only to assist the corporations that mine the gold but to assist those workers who invested their lives in the industry, and also the communities surrounding the industry. When a gold mine closes down the community is left, and so are many of the miners, with no assistance provided for them.

Mr. Speaker, I notice that the minister is in the chamber and I know he will listen to my remarks. In March of this year I made a speech on the subject of gold mines, especially those in northern Quebec, seeking extension of the subsidy on gold mining which was to be discontinued on December 31, 1970. Now a new approach has been taken and the subsidy will be paid until June, 1973. In my speech in March I emphasized that the municipalities in my constituency were very nervous about the prospects for the mining industry. We did not know whether the government was going to continue the subsidy. This is a situation which has existed since 1948, and every three years people have been sent from my constituency to plead with the government to continue the subsidy.

Mr. Speaker, representatives of many municipalities have submitted fairly long briefs to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) clearly showing the importance of gold mining in northwestern Quebec.
I appreciate the fact that the cost to the government of subsidizing gold mines is fairly high, since that has amounted to $280 million since 1948. On the other hand, it should not be forgotten that the citizens of the different mining communities pay taxes, unemployment insurance contributions, etc. If the government does the necessary computing, it will find, I am sure, that it is not the loser, since it has surely received millions in direct and indirect taxes.
Some 2,000 gold miners with their families live in northwestern Quebec. Consequently, the closing down of those mines would compel thousands of workers to migrate, and this would increase unemployment as these men are not trained for other work.
Mr. Speaker, experience has shown that retraining is not always possible for workers over 40 and, right now, almost 50 per cent of miners are 45 years old or over and about 75 per cent of them have less than 10 years of schooling.
As the representative of a region where the economy is based mainly on the mining industry, I know full well

that Canada could not do without that precious metal currently used in the making of various products. In fact, which of us does not own a gold watch, ring or chain?
The few millions the federal government gives this industry represent a real investment, because the importance of gold in private industry is forever increasing. Indeed, South African engineers say that industry will soon absorb almost all the gold produced.
Moreover, with grants to gold mines, the government is promoting exploration, which is essential. Everything possible should be done to ensure successful results.
Mr. Speaker, let us simply recall the good years when prospecting played an important part in the economy of northwestern Quebec. The Horne mine was discovered there and it is now the Noranda mine, one of the richest copper deposit in Canada.
One thing for sure, the problem we are discussing today will crop up again in 1973. I think that the federal government should endeavour to come up with a final solution to the problem of gold mining assistance. As I said earlier, stopping subsidies would create insurmountable difficulties in various areas of the province, particularly in northwestern Quebec.
One method has been suggested to counteract the closure of gold mines and that is to retrain the miners and grant them allowances enabling them to relocate where-they might work at their new trade. Unfortunately such a program would strangle the economy of mining towns where there would be nobody left but children and older people.

Mr. Speaker, I feel deeply honoured that we have two eminent environmental experts in our presence this evening in the person of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) and in the person of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene). Their presence almost
October 29, 1970

flabbergasts me because I am going to touch on a topic that demands a tremendous amount of expertise and I have only two or three minutes with which to scratch the surface.
It is encouraging to notice that in the area of oceanography, about which I raised this question with the Minister a couple of days ago, Canada by its efforts with Hudson 70 has been making some dramatic moves. It is also encouraging to read a report in the Globe and Mail on trilateral efforts by Canada, the Soviet Union and the United States in the area of research respecting herring resources on Canada's east coast.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I want to open up the question of the whole business of marine resources-not only the renewable resources but others such as oil, minerals and the like. I ask the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry if he could now for a few minutes, and later in a prepared statement, elaborate on Canada's present and future efforts in oceanography and matters to do with marine resources.
I have been reading a great deal of literature on this subject and I notice that most people writing on it today acknowledge that our marine resources are of much more value than our land resources. It startled me to learn that the offshore oil resources and the continental shelf resources as outlined at the 1958 Law of the Sea Conference at Geneva indicate that there may be as much as 300 billion barrels of oil as one type of resource. That is over and above fishing and what can be called renewable resources.
I have been reading a number of articles by eminent people in the field who feel that Canada, among the major marine nations of the world, has to regain lost ground in terms of oceanographic study. Rear Admiral Harry Porter, writing in the March, 1970, edition of Canadian Shipping in an article called "Seapower and Canada," said:
Today, much effort is being spent on oceanographic research -research into the biological content and chemical and physical properties of the sea. This work has major economic and military significance, and is of particular importance to the fishing industry. Canada carries out a modest program in this field, while the U.S. has a large program. The Russians have a research fleet that, in numbers, is larger than the rest of the world's put together.
I do not know if Rear Admiral Porter knows exactly what he is talking about, but I have checked him out and apparently he is a rather conservative individual, in the non-political sense. There is also an article by Mr. M. J. Colpitts, chief of the marine division of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, which appeared in the June/July, 1970, issue of Sea Harvest. In this he indicates practically the same conclusion and goes on to point out the efforts being made by a number of countries such as the United States with its 1966 Marine Resource and Development Act in order to give all its marine studies, oceanographic studies, and so on, a particular direction, a
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion specific and encompassing contribution. They feel it is very important to be in the vanguard in this area.
Great Britain in 1968 formed the Committee on Marine Technology, and also in 1968 France announced a program to tie together all the efforts they are making in this particular area. The Republic of Germany, which is one of the greatest predators of the fisheries on the east coast of Canada, in 1968 set up the German Commission for Oceanography. Six other nations, including France, constitute what was termed Eurocean. These six nations are trying to work together on oceanographic studies.
I raise the question because yesterday I had an opportunity to talk with a number of people at the United Nations who are expert in the field, regarding the Law of the Sea. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry has been saying we must have a vehicle for bringing about discussions and negotiations on our marine resources as they pertain to fishing, but these people tell me that they Eire only now in the stages of setting up a preparatory committee to find out if they will have such a conference, what the agenda will be and who will participate.
They tell me that the United States has assembled such a mass of information and such documentation on the business, and has accumulated ecological studies, mineral rights, territorial rights and so on, that it will take them about two years to find out exactly what the United States has presented. Indeed, they feel it is likely to take about five years before the preparatory work can be carried out for such a study. However, they feel it is physically possible within two years but could take as long as five. I look forward to hearing from the minister about the work he has done in the last few weeks with respect to the Soviet Union and Canada, and I hope he will tell us more about his plan for the east coast of Canada.
It seems that discussions along the lines that have taken place will form the burden of our activity in connection with marine technology. We are concerned about what happened on the west coast, where Canada held discussions in this area. We are so backward in this area that we cannot sit at the same table. The Russians, with all their men and vessels reached certain conclusions. Canada, renting a little submarine that was built in my riding, went down to the bottom to

I was surprised to hear the hon. member say that we are not spending money on oceanography. Canada has one of the world's best, if not the best, centres of oceanography at Bedford in the Halifax area. We are spending millions of dollars in oceanographic studies in the north Atlantic. We know a lot about fish in that area. We have some of the best people and best equipment. Coordination of our efforts will be better under the new department of environment which will bring together all matters in connection with our waters. I think we will be more effective in the future.
The agreement with the Russians on the west coast was possible as a result of our closing the port of Vancouver. If we had not done that, the Russians would not have come to us. When we closed the port, the Russians pleaded with us to let them have fresh water so that they would not have to travel 4,000 miles to Siberia. We said we would open the port if they got off the continental shelf. They agreed to do so. Perhaps the hon. member is pleading a similar case for the east coast. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the sympathy I feel for the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, I am afraid that my statement tonight will not give her nor her friends of the Viet Nam Committee the satisfaction they were looking for.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to hear that the planned march will take place. However, I would like to inform the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway that the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister have repeated time and again in this House and elsewhere that the War Measures Act proclaimed on October 16 was to apply only to the specific FLQ problem in Quebec. To the knowledge of the Justice Department, it would seem that Vancouver's Viet Nam Committee does not pursue the same objectives as the FLQ.
On the other hand, the implementation of the regulations provided for in the proclamation of October 16 is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Attorneys General of the provinces.
